claim: In birds and mammals the embryonic somites generate a linear series of impenetrable barriers, forcing axon growth cones to traverse one half of each somite as they extend towards their body targets.
source: In birds and mammals the embryonic somites generate a linear series of impenetrable barriers, forcing axon growth cones to traverse one half of each somite as they extend towards their body targets.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Protein disulphide isomerase provides a key component of somite barriers, mediating contact repulsion at the cell surface in chick half-somites.
source: This study shows that protein disulphide isomerase provides a key component of these barriers, mediating contact repulsion at the cell surface in chick half-somites.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including siRNA knockdown, pharmacological inhibition, and biochemical characterization.

claim: Repulsion is reduced both in vivo and in vitro by a range of methods that inhibit PDI enzyme activity.
source: Repulsion is reduced both in vivo and in vitro by a range of methods that inhibit enzyme activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments using PACMA 31, siRNA knockdown, and other PDI inhibitors shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PDI activity is critical in initiating a nitric oxide/S-nitrosylation-dependent signal transduction pathway that regulates the growth cone cytoskeleton.
source: The activity is critical in initiating a nitric oxide/S-nitrosylation-dependent signal transduction pathway that regulates the growth cone cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that PDI+GSNO induces growth cone collapse, that NO scavengers block this effect, and that LC1 is S-nitrosylated in somite extracts.

claim: Rat forebrain grey matter extracts contain a similar PDI activity to that found in somites.
source: Rat forebrain grey matter extracts contain a similar activity, and the enzyme is expressed at the surface of cultured human astrocytic cells and rat cortical astrocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assays showing that rat forebrain extracts induce growth cone collapse that is inhibited by PDI inhibitors (Figure 4).

claim: PDI is expressed at the surface of cultured human astrocytic cells and rat cortical astrocytes.
source: Rat forebrain grey matter extracts contain a similar activity, and the enzyme is expressed at the surface of cultured human astrocytic cells and rat cortical astrocytes.
evidence: This is shown by live-staining experiments on human 1718 astrocytic cells (Figure 4e) and Western blotting of rat cortical astrocyte cell surface preparations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).

claim: In avian and mammalian embryos, both outgrowing motor and sensory axons, and migrating neural crest cells, traverse preferentially the anterior (A, rostral/cranial) - rather than posterior (P, caudal) - halves of each successive somite.
source: In avian and mammalian embryos, both outgrowing motor and sensory axons, and migrating neural crest cells, encounter the periodic somites that flank both sides of the neural tube (future spinal cord). Here they traverse preferentially the anterior (A, rostral/cranial) - rather than posterior (P, caudal) - halves of each successive somite (Keynes and Stern, 1984; Rickmann et al., 1985; Bronner-Fraser, 1986; Fleming et al., 2015; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: For neural crest cells, the preference for anterior half-somites depends on repulsive signalling in the P-half-somite by members of the Semaphorin/Neuropilin- and Ephrin/Eph protein families.
source: For neural crest cells this preference has been shown to depend on repulsive signalling in the P-half-somite by members of the Semaphorin/Neuropilin- and Ephrin/Eph protein families (Krull et al., 1997; Wang and Anderson, 1997; Koblar et al., 2000; Gammill et al., 2006; Davy and Soriano, 2007; Schwarz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The basis of axonal segmental patterning has remained elusive.
source: However the basis of axonal segmental patterning has remained elusive.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Contact repulsion is the main cellular mechanism generating axonal patterning in somites.
source: We previously identified contact repulsion as the main cellular mechanism generating axonal patterning (Davies et al., 1990; Keynes et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors cited in the text.

claim: Sequential repulsion of outgrowing motor and sensory axons in successive P-half-sclerotomes forces axons to traverse the anterior (A/cranial) halves.
source: Sequential repulsion of outgrowing motor and sensory axons in successive P-half-sclerotomes (future vertebrae) forces axons to traverse the anterior (A/cranial) halves.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors and represents an established model.

claim: Extracts of chick embryo somites cause growth cone collapse of both motor and sensory axons in vitro.
source: We showed that extracts of chick embryo somites cause growth cone collapse of both motor and sensory axons in vitro (Davies et al., 1990), a phenomenon that is widely used as a method for identifying molecules that regulate growth cone motility (Kapfhammer and Raper, 1987; Raper and Kapfhammer, 1990).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors and is cited.

claim: The lectins peanut agglutinin (PNA) and jacalin bind selectively to the surface of P-half-sclerotome cells rather than A-half-sclerotome cells.
source: Additionally we found that the lectins peanut agglutinin (PNA) and jacalin bind selectively to the surface of P-half-sclerotome cells rather than A-half-sclerotome cells (Davies et al., 1990; Stern et al., 1986).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors and collaborators.

claim: Immobilized PNA can be used to deplete collapse activity from somite extracts, and activity is recovered by lactose elution.
source: Immobilized PNA can be used to deplete collapse activity, and activity is recovered by lactose elution.
evidence: This is based on previous biochemical work by the authors.

claim: Biochemical purification led to the identification of two PNA-binding glycoproteins shown by SDS-PAGE as two silver staining bands of 48 kDa and 55 kDa.
source: Biochemical purification led to the identification of two PNA-binding glycoproteins shown by SDS-PAGE as two silver staining bands of 48 kDa and 55 kDa (Davies et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: PNA affinity purification combined with more effective protease inhibition revealed a major silver-staining band of apparent molecular weight 57 kDa.
source: In the present work we combined PNA affinity purification with more effective inhibition of protease activity in the somite extracts, and examined the lactose eluates by semi-preparative SDS PAGE. This revealed a major silver-staining band of apparent molecular weight 57 kDa, closely matching the 55 kDa band seen in the earlier study (Davies et al., 1990; Figure 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b and represents new experimental data.

claim: The 57 kDa band was identified as protein disulphide isomerase/PDIA1/P4HB by mass spectrometry.
source: The band was excised and submitted for tryptic digestion and mass spectrometry, revealing 57 peptides distributed throughout the extent of the enzyme protein disulphide isomerase/PDIA1/P4HB (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: PDIA1/P4HB is one of a PDI-family of proteins that share in common a thioredoxin-like structural fold.
source: PDIA1/P4HB is one of a PDI-family of proteins that share in common a thioredoxin-like structural fold (Kozlov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PDIA1/P4HB is known principally as an intracellular enzyme localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where it regulates protein folding by catalyzing the formation and breakage of disulphide bonds.
source: It is known principally as an intracellular enzyme localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where it regulates protein folding by catalyzing the formation and breakage of disulphide bonds (Goldberger et al., 1963; Ali Khan and Mutus, 2014; Parakh and Atkin, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Somite cell surface PDI (csPDI) binds PNA and is lactose-elutable from immobilized PNA, indicating that this form of PDI is O-glycosylated.
source: Our finding that somite cell surface PDI (csPDI) binds PNA, and is lactose-elutable from immobilized PNA, indicates that this form of PDI is O-glycosylated.
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical properties of PNA binding and lactose elution.

claim: csPDI expressed by Jurkat T cells possesses PNA-binding O-glycans, the elongation of which can be blocked experimentally.
source: This is supported by the observation that csPDI expressed by Jurkat T cells, immortalized from human T cell leukaemia, also possesses PNA-binding O-glycans, the elongation of which can be blocked experimentally (Bi et al., 2011; Schaefer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Commercially purified (bovine liver) PDI does not bind to PNA-agarose, indicating that somite csPDI has an affinity for PNA based on its glycosylation state.
source: In addition, using a sensitive fluorescent reductase assay (Raturi and Mutus, 2007) we found that commercially purified (bovine liver) PDI does not bind to PNA-agarose, indicating that somite csPDI has an affinity for PNA based on its glycosylation state (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: PDI expression at the surface of P-half-sclerotome cells was confirmed by live-staining of microdissected strips of chick somites using both polyclonal anti-PDI antibody and fluorescently labelled PNA, which showed co-localization at the cell periphery.
source: The expression of PDI at the surface of P-half-sclerotome cells was confirmed by live-staining of microdissected strips of chick somites, using both polyclonal anti-PDI antibody and fluorescently labelled PNA, which showed co-localization at the cell periphery in the P-half-sclerotome (Figure 1c–g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1c-g.

claim: The onset of PNA staining in the P-half-sclerotome precedes the first emergence of motor and sensory axon outgrowth in the A-half-sclerotome by ~1.5–3 hr.
source: Also the onset of PNA staining in the P-half-sclerotome was found to precede the first emergence of motor and sensory axon outgrowth in the A-half-sclerotome by ~1.5–3 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by temporal analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: PDI knockdown in ovo caused loss of extracellular PNA-binding in P-half-sclerotomes.
source: As predicted however, PDI knockdown in ovo caused loss of extracellular PNA-binding in P-half-sclerotomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e-g.

claim: PDI knockdown caused outgrowing motor axons to project additionally into the P-half-sclerotomes adjacent to the neural tube/spinal cord.
source: However PDI knockdown caused outgrowing motor axons to project additionally into the P-half-sclerotomes adjacent to the neural tube/spinal cord (Figure 2c,d), an abnormal trajectory not seen in untreated embryos or in those similarly treated with control/scrambled siRNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Expression of the A-half-somite polarity determinant gene Tbx18 was unaffected by siRNA injection.
source: Control experiments showed that expression of the A-half-somite polarity determinant gene Tbx18 was unaffected by siRNA injection, whereas expression of the P-half determinant gene Uncx4.1 was variably diminished in the treated region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Expression of the P-half determinant gene Uncx4.1 was variably diminished in the siRNA-treated region.
source: Control experiments showed that expression of the A-half-somite polarity determinant gene Tbx18 was unaffected by siRNA injection, whereas expression of the P-half determinant gene Uncx4.1 was variably diminished in the treated region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Co-injection of siRNA with a FLAG-M1-epitope-tagged plasmid expressing human PDIA1/P4HB partially rescued the normal segmented axon phenotype.
source: To rule out the possibility that these phenotypes resulted from an off-target effect of the siRNA, control experiments confirmed that co-injection of siRNA with a FLAG-M1-epitope-tagged plasmid expressing human PDIA1/P4HB (>90% homologous to chicken PDIA1 Everson and Kao, 1997) partially rescued the normal segmented axon phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i–k).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i-k.

claim: PACMA 31 forms a covalent bond with a cysteine residue of the second active site of PDI, thereby inhibiting its catalytic activity.
source: PDI possesses two independent active sites, and the small molecule PACMA 31 has been shown to form a covalent bond with a cysteine residue of the second active site, thereby inhibiting its catalytic activity (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: PACMA 31 injection caused abnormal axon projections into P-half-sclerotome whereas control/PACMA 56 injection did not.
source: Consistent with the results of siRNA knockdown, PACMA 31 injection also caused abnormal axon projections into P-half-sclerotome whereas control/PACMA 56 injection did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1l–n).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1l-n.

claim: The A-P width of ventral roots increased after PACMA 31 injection, indicating axon defasciculation.
source: In addition the A-P width of ventral roots increased after PACMA 31 injection, indicating axon defasciculation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1o).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1o.

claim: PACMA 31 bead implantation caused abnormal axon outgrowth into P-half-somite territory in 14/29 embryos.
source: As with siRNA knockdown, PACMA 31 caused abnormal axon outgrowth into P-half-somite territory (Figure 2e,f; 14/29 embryos).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 2e,f.

claim: Using PACMA 56 as control, only an occasional axon outgrowth abnormality (1/20 embryos) was observed.
source: Using PACMA 56 as control, only an occasional axon outgrowth abnormality (1/20 embryos) was observed; in 19/20 embryos, axons were confined to the A-half-sclerotomes as in normal embryos (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Purified bovine PDI incorporated in liposomes at concentrations of 25–1000 ng/ml did not increase growth cone collapse above control levels.
source: The purified bovine enzyme incorporated in liposomes was added at a range of concentrations (25–1000 ng/ml) to cultures of chick embryo dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) extending sensory axons on laminin in the presence of nerve growth factor (NGF; typically between 50 to >100 growth cones were assayed per DRG). However this did not increase collapse above the control levels (0–20% of growth cones) seen after addition of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) or untreated liposomes (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Application of GSNO alone in solution did not elicit growth cone collapse above control levels.
source: Whereas application of GSNO alone in solution did not elicit collapse above control levels, significant collapse was observed when GSNO was first combined with PDI (125 ng/ml) and then added to DRG cultures (~60% growth cones collapsed after 1 hr, Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Significant growth cone collapse was observed when GSNO was combined with PDI (125 ng/ml) (~60% growth cones collapsed after 1 hr).
source: Whereas application of GSNO alone in solution did not elicit collapse above control levels, significant collapse was observed when GSNO was first combined with PDI (125 ng/ml) and then added to DRG cultures (~60% growth cones collapsed after 1 hr, Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: The PDI concentration dependence of collapse was similar when PDI+GSNO was applied in solution or in liposomes.
source: To confirm that PDI+GSNO-induced collapse in solution is reproduced in the liposome-based collapse assay, we found that the PDI concentration dependence of collapse was similar in both cases. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,c.

claim: The time course of PDI+GSNO-induced collapse was similar to that induced by somite extracts, and contrasted with the more rapid onset of collapse induced by the soluble repellent Sema3A.
source: Also the time course of PDI+GSNO-induced collapse was similar to that induced by somite extracts, and contrasted with the more rapid onset of collapse induced by the soluble repellent Sema3A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time course data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-f.

claim: Bacitracin, anti-PDI neutralizing antibody and PAO were most effective in reducing PDI+GSNO-induced collapse when incorporated in liposomes with PDI.
source: Of these, three inhibitors (bacitracin, neutralizing antibody and PAO) were most effective in reducing collapse when incorporated in liposomes with PDI (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g–l).
evidence: This is demonstrated by inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g-l.

claim: PACMA 31 in liposomes inhibited somite extract-induced collapse by >50% whereas PACMA 56 was inactive.
source: Following the publication of the small molecule PDI-inhibitor PACMA 31 and its control PACMA 56 (Xu et al., 2012), the candidacy of csPDI in mediating somite extract (SE)-induced collapse was further confirmed using PACMA 31 in liposomes, which inhibited collapse by >50% whereas PACMA 56 was inactive (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: PDI has two active sites, each with the amino acid sequence WCGHCK.
source: PDI has two active sites, each with the amino acid sequence WCGHCK.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDI structure.

claim: PDI can be S-nitrosylated (PDI-SNO), and the enzyme can also act as a denitrosylase resulting in •NO release as a free radical.
source: Sliskovic et al., 2005 have shown that PDI can be S-nitrosylated (PDI-SNO), and that the enzyme can also act as a denitrosylase resulting in •NO release as a free radical.
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: PDI-SNO is denitrosylated by a one-electron reduction mechanism at the second active site.
source: They have proposed that PDI-SNO is denitrosylated by a one-electron reduction mechanism at the second active site.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal from cited work.

claim: Glutathione (GSH) is the most effective reducing agent for PDI denitrosylation, and no significant denitrosylation is observed using reducing agents dithiothreitol (DTT) or L-homocysteine.
source: Moreover they showed that glutathione (GSH) is the most effective reducing agent, and that no significant denitrosylation is observed using reducing agents dithiothreitol (DTT) or L-homocysteine (Sliskovic et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: When PDI+GSNO or somite extracts were incorporated in liposomes and subsequently treated with GSH (3 mM), collapse activity was lost.
source: Consistent with their study, we found that when PDI+GSNO or somite extracts were incorporated in liposomes and subsequently treated with GSH (3 mM), collapse activity was lost.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data consistent with cited work.

claim: Identical experiments using 3 mM DTT or L-homocysteine did not affect collapse activity.
source: However identical experiments using 3 mM DTT or L-homocysteine did not affect collapse activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: GSH did not block collapse when applied at 3 µM, within the extracellular concentration range typically present in vivo.
source: Notably, GSH did not block collapse when applied at 3 µM, within the extracellular concentration range typically present in vivo and 3 orders of magnitude below the ambient intracellular concentration range (Owen and Butterfield, 2010; Figure 3d; see Discussion).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and supported by citation.

claim: Somite extract-induced collapse was inhibited by 3 mM GSH but not by 3 mM L-homocysteine.
source: Also consistent with the observations of Sliskovic et al., 2005., somite extract-induced collapse was inhibited by 3 mM GSH but not by 3 mM L-homocysteine (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Myoglobin inhibited collapse induced by PDI+GSNO and by somite extracts.
source: Further evidence that a NO-based mechanism elicits growth cone collapse was provided by the finding that myoglobin, regarded as a pseudo-enzymatic NO scavenger (Ascenzi and Brunori, 2001; Rayner et al., 2009), inhibited collapse induced by PDI+GSNO and by somite extracts (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: PDI+GSNO-induced collapse was inhibited by the membrane-impermeable NO-scavenger carboxy-2-Phenyl-4,4,5,5-tetramethylimidazoline-1-oxyl 3-oxide (C-PTIO).
source: PDI+GNSO-induced collapse was also inhibited by the membrane-impermeable NO-scavenger carboxy-2-Phenyl-4,4,5,5-tetramethylimidazoline-1-oxyl 3-oxide (C-PTIO; Figure 3g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Somite extract-induced collapse was prevented by pre-treatment of DRGs with the neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) inhibitor L-NAME, but not by its control/chiral isomer D-NAME.
source: Somite extract-induced collapse was additionally prevented by pre-treatment of DRGs with the neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) inhibitor L-NAME, but not by its control/chiral isomer D-NAME, indicating a role for nNOS activity in the collapse process (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: S-nitrosylation of Cys 2457 in the MAP1B light chain sub-unit (LC1) is a critical event in the cytoskeletal dynamics underlying growth cone collapse.
source: The in vitro study of Stroissnigg et al., 2007 has likewise shown a role for S-nitrosylation of the microtubule-associated protein MAP1B in mediating mouse DRG growth cone collapse caused by stimulation of nNOS by the calcium ionophore calcimycin/A23187. They showed further that S-nitrosylation of Cys 2457 in the MAP1B light chain sub-unit (LC1) is a critical event in the cytoskeletal dynamics underlying collapse.
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: Only one major band (molecular weight 38 kDa) was detectably S-nitrosylated in cell-free somite extracts.
source: Remarkably only one major band (molecular weight 38 kDa) was detectably S-nitrosylated (Figure 3i).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: The S-nitrosylated 38 kDa somite protein reacts strongly with anti-LC1 antibody.
source: We additionally confirmed, by Western blotting using a mouse monoclonal antibody against amino acids 2257–2357 in LC1 of mouse MAP-1B (see Materials and methods), that this S-nitrosylated somite protein reacts strongly with the anti-LC1 antibody (Figure 3j).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The nNOS inhibitor L-NAME inhibited both S-nitrosylation of the 38 kDa protein and somite extract-induced growth cone collapse, while the control stereoisomer D-NAME was without effect.
source: Also the nNOS inhibitor L-NAME inhibited both S-nitrosylation of the 38 kDa protein (Figure 3k) and somite extract-induced growth cone collapse (Figure 3h), while the control stereoisomer D-NAME was without effect (Figure 3h,k).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blotting and collapse assay data shown in Figures 3h and 3k.

claim: Extracts of adult mammalian and chicken forebrain grey matter cause sensory/DRG axon growth cone collapse that can be depleted by the use of immobilized PNA.
source: We previously found that, as for somites, extracts of adult mammalian and chicken forebrain grey matter also cause sensory/DRG axon growth cone collapse that can be depleted by the use of immobilized PNA.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Immobilized jacalin can be used to deplete collapse induced by rat forebrain extracts (RFE).
source: In confirmation we found that immobilized jacalin, a lectin that binds the same O-linked disaccharide (Galβ1-3GalNAc) as does PNA, but unlike PNA is not selective for its de-sialylation, can be used to deplete collapse induced by rat forebrain extracts (RFE; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Application of PACMA 31 (5μM) significantly reduced RFE-induced collapse (by 50–60%) whereas PACMA 56 (5μM) did not.
source: Application of PACMA 31 (5μM) significantly reduced collapse (by 50–60%) whereas PACMA 56 (5μM) did not (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Quercetin-3-O-rutinoside inhibited RFE-induced collapse when used at both 1 μM and 50 μM.
source: Another small molecule PDI-inhibitor, quercetin-3-O-rutinoside (Jasuja et al., 2012) inhibited RFE-induced collapse when used at both 1 μM and 50 μM (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: RFE-induced collapse activity was immunodepleted using polyclonal anti-PDI antibody but not using IgG or bovine serum albumin (BSA) as sham protein controls.
source: RFE-induced collapse activity was immunodepleted using polyclonal anti-PDI antibody but not using IgG or bovine serum albumin (BSA) as sham protein controls (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunodepletion experiments shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Application of 3 mM GSH reduced RFE-induced growth cone collapse, whereas 3 mM DTT, 3 mM L-homocysteine (L-HC) or 3 μM GSH did not.
source: Moreover, as for somite extracts, application of 3 mM GSH reduced RFE-induced growth cone collapse, whereas 3 mM DTT, 3 mM L-homocysteine (L-HC) or 3 μM GSH did not (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: At GSH concentrations between 3 μM and 3 mM, inhibition of RFE-induced collapse increased with concentration.
source: At GSH concentrations between 3 μM and 3 mM, inhibition of collapse increased with concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Application of the NO scavengers myoglobin and C-PTIO depleted RFE-induced collapse.
source: Last, and again consistent with a NO-based mechanism, we confirmed that application of the NO scavengers myoglobin and C-PTIO depleted RFE-induced collapse (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: The astrocyte shares fate specification by the transcription factor SOX9 with P-half-sclerotome cells (future vertebral cartilage).
source: One source of csPDI in the brain may be the astrocyte, which shares fate specification by the transcription factor SOX9 with P-half-sclerotome cells (future vertebral cartilage) (Akiyama et al., 2002; Stolt et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established by citations to previous work.

claim: csPDI is expressed on the surface of cultured human astrocytic cells.
source: In support of this, live-staining experiments showed that csPDI is expressed on the surface of cultured human astrocytic cells, as for P-half-sclerotome cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Extracts of human astrocytic cells caused growth cone collapse that was removed by the use of immobilized PNA and jacalin.
source: Moreover extracts of these cells caused growth cone collapse that was removed by the use of immobilized PNA and jacalin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f), and a cell surface preparation isolated from rat primary cortical astrocytes was found to contain csPDI (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay and Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f,g.

claim: A cell surface preparation isolated from rat primary cortical astrocytes contains csPDI.
source: Moreover extracts of these cells caused growth cone collapse that was removed by the use of immobilized PNA and jacalin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f), and a cell surface preparation isolated from rat primary cortical astrocytes was found to contain csPDI (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g.

claim: NGF-dependent primary sensory neurons project axons in vivo in the CNS as well as PNS, making synapses in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and in the brainstem.
source: The NGF-dependent primary sensory neurons assessed here project axons in vivo in the CNS as well as PNS, making synapses in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and in the brainstem.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Two populations of CNS-restricted neurons (telencephalic and retinal) are responsive to the somite contact-repellent system.
source: We have shown previously that two populations of CNS-restricted neurons are also responsive to the somite contact-repellent system. When explants of embryonic day-4 (E4) chick telencephalon or E7 retina are grafted in ovo in place of chick spinal cord, their axons avoid P-half-somites (Keynes et al., 1991; Vermeren et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Chick retinal axon growth cones collapse in response to somite extracts in vitro.
source: Moreover chick retinal axon growth cones collapse in response to somite extracts in vitro (Vermeren et al., 2000), and in further confirmation we found that they collapse in response to PDI+GSNO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h and supported by citation.

claim: Chick retinal axon growth cones collapse in response to PDI+GSNO.
source: Moreover chick retinal axon growth cones collapse in response to somite extracts in vitro (Vermeren et al., 2000), and in further confirmation we found that they collapse in response to PDI+GSNO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Contact between a single DRG growth cone filopodium and the surface of a P-half-somite cell in vitro is sufficient to initiate a rapid filopodial withdrawal/repulsive response, followed by reorientation of the growth cone away from the cell.
source: In keeping with this, it has been shown that contact between a single DRG growth cone filopodium and the surface of a P-half-somite cell in vitro is sufficient to initiate a rapid filopodial withdrawal/repulsive response, followed by reorientation of the growth cone away from the cell (Steketee and Tosney, 1999).
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: Cell viability is unperturbed despite inhibition of csPDI expression.
source: However we used the same target for gene knockdown experiments as used by Zai et al., 1999., who showed that cell viability is unperturbed despite inhibition of csPDI expression.
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: In chick somites the onset of csPDI expression in P-half-sclerotome immediately precedes the first emergence of spinal axons in the A-half.
source: In chick somites the onset of csPDI expression in P-half-sclerotome immediately precedes the first emergence of spinal axons in the A-half.
evidence: This is demonstrated by temporal analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: The selective migration of neural crest cells in A-half-sclerotomes precedes by several hours the first axon outgrowth at each segmental level in the chick embryo.
source: The selective migration of neural crest cells in A-half-sclerotomes precedes by several hours the first axon outgrowth at each segmental level in the chick embryo, and is likewise matched temporally by the onset of expression of the secreted repellent Sema3F in newly-formed P-half-sclerotomes (Gammill et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: The secreted axon repellent protein Sema3A is expressed selectively in P-half-sclerotome.
source: The secreted axon repellent protein Sema3A is additionally expressed selectively in P-half-sclerotome (Eickholt et al., 1999) (see also Shepherd et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established by citations to previous work.

claim: No long-distance axon repulsion is detected in collagen gel co-explants of DRGs with dissected P-half-sclerotomes.
source: However no long-distance axon repulsion is detected in collagen gel co-explants of DRGs with dissected P-half-sclerotomes (Keynes et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Segmented spinal nerve patterning persists in compound Neuropilin1/2 mutant mice in which somite-based Semaphorin signalling is depleted.
source: Moreover, segmented spinal nerve patterning persists in compound Neuropilin1/2 mutant mice in which somite-based Semaphorin signalling is depleted (Schwarz et al., 2009; Huber et al., 2005), presumably because csPDI expression in these mice compensates disrupted neural crest migration.
evidence: This is established by citations to previous work, with an inference about the compensatory role of csPDI.

claim: The segmental patterning of neural crest cells and axons is regulated predominantly by distinct molecular signals.
source: Together these observations imply that the segmental patterning of neural crest cells and axons is regulated predominantly by distinct molecular signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Semaphorin signaling affects neural crest but not axon patterning, while PDI affects axon patterning.

claim: The Eph-family receptor tyrosine kinase EphB2 and its ligand ephrin-B1 have been implicated in somite-based repulsion of neural crest cells but are not necessary for motor axon segmentation.
source: Supporting this, the Eph-family receptor tyrosine kinase EphB2 and its ligand ephrin-B1 have been additionally implicated in somite-based repulsion of neural crest cells (Krull et al., 1997; Wang and Anderson, 1997; Davy and Soriano, 2007), but shown not to be necessary for motor axon segmentation (Koblar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established by citations to previous work.

claim: csPDI acts as a de-nitrosylase, operating constitutively at the P-half-somite cell surface to promote the transfer of NO• from extracellular S-nitrosothiols into the cytosol of contacting growth cone filopodia, thereby initiating repulsion/collapse.
source: We suggest that csPDI acts as a de-nitrosylase, operating constitutively at the P-half-somite cell surface to promote the transfer of NO• from extracellular S-nitrosothiols into the cytosol of contacting growth cone filopodia, thereby initiating repulsion/collapse (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Extracellular S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) may provide a ubiquitous source of NO donor.
source: Extracellular S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) may provide a ubiquitous source of NO donor, as suggested for csPDI activity in the context of platelet aggregation (Shah et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to previous work in a different context.

claim: The ambient extracellular concentration of GSNO in vivo (~1 µM) is sufficient, in combination with purified PDI, to elicit growth cone collapse in vitro.
source: Critically we have shown that its ambient extracellular concentration in vivo (~1 µM) is sufficient, in combination with purified PDI, to elicit growth cone collapse in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by collapse assay experiments using physiologically relevant concentrations.

claim: S-nitrosylation of LC1 induces a conformational change that enhances binding of the LC1-HC complex to microtubules, blocking dynein action and promoting retraction over extension.
source: Our results accord well with the proposal of Stroissnigg et al., 2007 that, in axons extending in vitro, growth cone retraction is counteracted by a microtubule/dynein-based system. S-nitrosylation of LC1 induces a conformational change that enhances binding of the LC1-HC complex to microtubules, so blocking dynein action and promoting retraction over extension.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model from cited work that is consistent with the authors' findings.

claim: Motor and sensory axon growth cones extending at the A/P-half-somite boundaries will make filopodial contact with P-half-somite cells expressing csPDI, triggering NO-mediated repulsive signalling.
source: Correspondingly, in the somite system in vivo both motor and sensory axon growth cones extending at the A/P-half-somite boundaries will make filopodial contact with P-half-somite cells expressing csPDI, triggering NO-mediated repulsive signalling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings about csPDI expression and mechanism.

claim: LC1 is the only S-nitrosylated protein detected in cell free extracts of dissected somite strips.
source: Consistent with this, using the iodo-TMT reagent we find that LC1 is the only S-nitrosylated protein detected in cell free extracts of dissected somite strips, which necessarily include growth cone proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3i,j.

claim: A broad range of CNS axon types may prove susceptible to csPDI-mediated repulsion.
source: In view of the involvement of NO/S-nitrosylation signalling in the csPDI-mediated repulsion mechanism, rather than a protein-based ligand-receptor interaction, a broad range of CNS axon types may prove susceptible to it.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the mechanism identified.

claim: csPDI expression by human malignant glioblastoma cells has been related to their invasiveness within the brain.
source: It may also be significant that csPDI expression by human malignant glioblastoma cells has been related to their invasiveness within the brain (Goplen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established by citation to previous work.

claim: A recent proteomic analysis identified csPDI/P4HB among the most enriched candidates at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses in embryonic rat cortical neuronal cultures.
source: The neuron may be another source of brain-derived csPDI, since a recent proteomic analysis of CNS synaptic cleft proteins identified csPDI/P4HB among the most enriched candidates at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses in embryonic rat cortical neuronal cultures Loh et al., 2016; csPDI has also been identified at the surface of both neuroblastoma cells (Xiao et al., 1999) and retinal cells (Pariser et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established by citations to previous work.

claim: csPDI has been identified at the surface of both neuroblastoma cells and retinal cells.
source: The neuron may be another source of brain-derived csPDI, since a recent proteomic analysis of CNS synaptic cleft proteins identified csPDI/P4HB among the most enriched candidates at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses in embryonic rat cortical neuronal cultures Loh et al., 2016; csPDI has also been identified at the surface of both neuroblastoma cells (Xiao et al., 1999) and retinal cells (Pariser et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established by citations to previous work.

claim: csPDI may be 'bifunctional' in promoting both adhesive and repulsive neuronal/glial interactions in the CNS.
source: Together with the experiments reported in this study, these findings collectively raise the possibility that csPDI is 'bifunctional' in promoting both adhesive and repulsive neuronal/glial interactions in the CNS.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the diverse findings about csPDI.

claim: NO signalling is implicated in synapse elimination during CNS development.
source: For example, NO signalling is implicated in synapse elimination during CNS development (Wu et al., 1994; Gibbs and Truman, 1998), and csPDI activity might provide an extracellular source of NO alongside intracellular nNOS activity.
evidence: This is established by citations to previous work.

claim: csPDI activity might provide an extracellular source of NO alongside intracellular nNOS activity during synapse elimination.
source: For example, NO signalling is implicated in synapse elimination during CNS development (Wu et al., 1994; Gibbs and Truman, 1998), and csPDI activity might provide an extracellular source of NO alongside intracellular nNOS activity.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential role of csPDI.
